topics: Benchmark review: p50/p95/p99 latency and token throughput
Burst capacity planning and cost tradeoffs
KV/prefix cache impacts on cold-start latency
transcript:
[00:00] Aisha Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, and we can jump into the POC numbers.
[00:12] Mark Li: Hey Aisha, Mark here, Priya and Jonas also on our side.
[00:18] Aisha Patel: Great. Daniel from our SE team, do you want to run the numbers?
[00:22] Daniel Kim: Yeah, sure. So last week we ran the steady-state and burst benches, the spreadsheet I uploaded is 'dedicated-sizing-v3.xlsx' - link in the deck. High-level, your 8-GPU pool with x2 batching gave about 60 tokens/sec per GPU on the 7B quantized variant. P95 latency stayed around 320ms for 256-token responses under steady load.
[00:45] Priya Nambiar: Sorry, can you repeat the p95 number? I think I heard three-twenty.
[00:49] Daniel Kim: Yep, p95 ~320ms steady-state for the 256 token payload. When we simulated burst at 2x concurrent RPS without warm KV cache, the p95 jumped to ~750ms and p99 to ~1.3s.
[01:10] Jonas Becker: That jump is bigger than we expected. Is that cold KV cache effect or scheduling?
[01:15] Daniel Kim: Mostly cold KV / cold KV cache and some scheduling overhead - we saw queue depth spikes. Our profiling shows the KV cache hit rate for your workload was only 28% in that test because prompts have variable prefixes.
[01:33] Mark Li: Right, our prompts are fairly heterogeneous. We've tried aggressive prefixing but tradeoffs with accuracy.
[01:40] Aisha Patel: Important callout - caching helps a lot for stable prefixes. If cache hit goes to ~60%, p95 drops to about 380ms even in bursts.
[01:50] Priya Nambiar: Question on autoscaling: are the triggers based on GPU util or token queue depth? We want something that avoids scaling flapping.
[01:58] Daniel Kim: Good question. We recommend token-queue-depth + rolling window CPU and GPU util. In practice we do a 30s smoothing window and require sustained threshold breaches for 90s before scale-up to avoid thrash.
[02:12] Aisha Patel: Also we can do proactive burst capacity - reserve a small warm buffer of extra instances that can accept short bursts without cold starts. That's the burst pool idea.
[02:22] Mark Li: The cost of reserved warm buffers is my team's main worry. If we reserve 2 extra GPUs that sit idle 90% of the time it may be expensive.
[02:31] Daniel Kim: Totally. That's why we suggested a hybrid: reserved minimal warm pool (1 GPU) + vertical autoscale spike for immediate demand with fast startup optimizations (quantized weights in local NVMe cache). That tends to hit a good cost/latency sweet spot.
[02:48] Priya Nambiar: How fast are those fast-starts realistically? I thought model cold load times were multiple minutes.
[02:54] Daniel Kim: Full cold loads can be long, but with our model prefetch + partial weight paging and quantized kernels we can get into serving state in ~25-45s for the 7B model on your hardware. The warm buffer is still helpful for the first few seconds of spike.
[03:10] Jonas Becker: What about pre-warming via predictive scaling, like time-of-day triggers? We have weekday peaks at 11am-1pm typically.
[03:18] Daniel Kim: Yes, time-based scheduled scale-ups are a low-cost win. You can schedule to add capacity 5-10 minutes before expected windows. For unexpected spikes, the hybrid approach helps.
[03:26] Mark Li: Ok. Can you remind us the cost delta between doing a 8-GPU steady pool vs 6-GPU plus burst reserve?
[03:31] Daniel Kim: Per our sheet: 8-GPU steady is roughly 15% higher monthly committed cost but yields lower average latency and simpler autoscaling. 6-GPU + burst reserve (1 warm + autoscale) reduces committed spend by ~12% but expect occasional higher p95 during large bursts unless prefix hit-rate improves. Numbers in column D of the spreadsheet.
[03:53] Priya Nambiar: On security, we had a Q earlier about Private deployment or VPC egress. If we go Dedicated, our data still leaves our VPC? I want to confirm the networking model.
[04:03] Aisha Patel: For Dedicated we offer a customer-dedicated pool with private networking - traffic can stay inside your VPC when you choose the VPC peering option. We'll share the network diagram again.
[04:12] Mark Li: Good. For compliance we need audit logs and KMS integration - are those available on Dedicated now?
[04:19] Sofia Torres: Yes - audit logs, KMS integration, and RBAC are supported. There are a few enterprise features that require the Private plan but Dedicated covers the basics you asked about.
[04:28] Mark Li: Nice. Back to benchmarks - Aisha, you mentioned a 60 tokens/sec per GPU figure. Is that measured with continuous batching?
[04:36] Daniel Kim: It's with continuous batching plus a small preference for lower-latency batch sizes. We bias batch windows to 30ms up to a max batch of 8. That gives better p95 tradeoffs.
[04:47] Priya Nambiar: Can we tweak the batching window dynamically? Some of our workloads are latency-sensitive while others can tolerate batching.
[04:54] Daniel Kim: Yes, the runtime supports per-route batching configs. You can set stricter latency routes with smaller windows, and scale those to dedicated instances if needed.
[05:02] Jonas Becker: Any gotchas for autoscaling down? We don't want to lose cached KV state on scale-downs, causing a spike when it flips back up.
[05:11] Daniel Kim: Right - scale-down windows need to be conservative and you can pin some cache-holding instances. Also we have a policy to drain connections and warm-snapshot KV to a shared cache before decommissioning; it's not perfect but helps.
[05:26] Mark Li: What's our recommended scale-down cool-down?
[05:29] Daniel Kim: 10 minutes baseline, 15 for heavy KV use.
[05:33] Aisha Patel: Quick interjection - last week's experiment you did around 4x long prompts had interesting cost numbers. Daniel, can you summarize?
[05:40] Daniel Kim: Sure. Long prompt loads increase GPU memory pressure, reducing effective batch sizes; token throughput dropped by ~30% and p99 increased disproportionately. For these workloads we recommend either a larger instance class per GPU or shard the model variants and route long-prompt traffic to a variant with longer-sequence optimized kernels.
[05:59] Priya Nambiar: Sharding sounds complex for us operationally. Is there a simpler knob?
[06:04] Daniel Kim: You can also implement prompt-length based routing - if prompt > 1024 tokens, route to a dedicated pool sized for long sequences. It's less complex than sharding and effective.
[06:14] Mark Li: Ok, looking at risk, what's the timeline to go from POC to Dedicated contract if we like the results? We have procurement calendar in July.
[06:21] Aisha Patel: If the pilot hits targets we can move to a Dedicated contract within 3-4 weeks; procurement usually needs the SOW and SOC2 docs which we can share today.
[06:30] Priya Nambiar: Can you re-send the SOC2 and the deployment SOW link?
[06:34] Aisha Patel: Yeah, I'll include both in the follow-up email.
[06:37] [10:00] Mark Li: (laughter) sorry, time travel timestamp, ignore -
[06:42] Daniel Kim: (laughs) noted.
[06:45] Aisha Patel: Alright, let's step through the open action items. Daniel, you'll send the updated latency/cost sheet with the hybrid autoscale options.
[06:53] Daniel Kim: Yep, I'll include recommended triggers (queue depth 200 tokens, GPU util 75%, sustained 90s), suggested warm pool size 1 GPU, and scheduled scale windows for 11:00-13:00 weekdays.
[07:06] Priya Nambiar: For the burst test - we'll do 2x RPS spike and report back. Should we use the staging harness you provided?
[07:14] Daniel Kim: Please use the harness; it simulates realistic prompt distributions including the heterogeneous prefixes which are important for cache results.
[07:20] Jonas Becker: We'll try to run it Wednesday.
[07:23] Mark Li: Can we also get a quick runbook for interpreting the graphs? Last time we misread the token drop as infra failure when it was batching shift.
[07:31] Sofia Torres: I'll attach a short runbook with the follow-up.
[07:34] Priya Nambiar: One more quick question - does Redwood support per-tenant rate limiting inside Dedicated, so we can isolate noisy customers?
[07:42] Daniel Kim: Yes, per-route and per-API-key throttles are supported, and you can put stricter limits per downstream tenant.
[07:48] Mark Li: Great. Any other risks?
[07:50] Aisha Patel: Main risks are cache hit variability and procurement timeline. Both manageable.
[07:55] Mark Li: Ok, sounds good. Let's summarize next steps.
[07:58] Aisha Patel: Next steps: Daniel sends updated spreadsheet by 2026-06-12; Priya to provision staging and run burst test by 2026-06-15; Aisha to follow procurement and send SOC2/SOW. We'll reconvene 2026-06-16 if needed.
[08:14] Priya Nambiar: Works for me. Thanks everyone.
[08:17] Mark Li: Thanks.
[45:30] [END]
